catalog_quote: Bray 1909 sec. 11: "The main accent, which is for the most part not particularly decisive — only a shoii [scanned: short] included vowel in a suffix being entirely unaccented — falls ordinarily on the root of the word, though it is apt to be attracted to a syllable containing a long vowel or ending in a doubled consonant. In emphatic conversation, of course, the accent becomes definitely marked." Bray sec. 203: "In a few cases the accent is diverted from the base to the terminations, the vowel of which becomes long in consequence ... Thus; hunev, I may eat; kahes, thou mayst die". Andronov 1980: "Short and long vowels are the easiest to distinguish in stressed syllables (the stress generally falls on a long syllable). In words containing several long vowels the unstressed long vowels are often reduced quantitatively till they become short. ... Brahui stress is quantitative-dynamic and weak.…

audit.recode_to: Conditional only: if Elfenbein 1997 states categorically 'stress on the first long vowel/diphthong, otherwise on the first syllable' without geminate/cluster attraction or hedges, kind would move from weight-hedged to unhedged quantity-sensitive (unbounded, leftmost heavy else leftmost/initial) with wcls CVV rather than CVV+CVC; keep Bray sec. 203 / Bashir verb-form shifts as lexical-morphological exceptions.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three deciding passages are verbatim in the held scanned files at the stated djvu line locators (Bray sec. 11 lines 1703-1709, sec. 203 lines 7340ff; Andronov 1980 lines 76-91); only trivial scanned normalizations. (2) The coding rests on the standard reference grammar (Bray 1909, 242 pp) plus an independent Soviet grammar (Andronov 1980), which agree; open-text grade is honest. But Glottolog lists a dedicated phonology (Elfenbein 1997, 797-811) and a 1998 Routledge sketch that we do not hold, and two open secondary sources fetched sources today (Syed et al. 2022 Phonetica, citing Elfenbein 1997b; Wikipedia citing Krishnamurti 2003) attribute to that literature a crisper, unhedged rule (long vowel, else first syllable) with no mention of geminate-closed syllables. That could shift 'weight-hedged' to plain QS and narrow the heavy class, so the record is adequate rather than well-sour

sources.citation: Syed, Nasir A., Abdul Waheed Shah, Anqi Xu & Yi Xu. 2022. Post-focus compression in Brahvi and Balochi. Phonetica 79(2): 189-218. doi:10.1515/phon-2022-2020 (accepted MS from UCL homepage)
sources.quote: 'neither language has contrastive lexical stress in the narrow sense of using it to distinguish words (Elfenbein, 1997a, 1997b; ...). ... For Brahvi, stress falls on a long vowel in a word, but on the first syllable in words consisting of only short syllables (Elfenbein, 1997b).' Instrumental part concerns focus (PFC), not word stress.

sources.citation: Bashir, Elena. 2010. Innovations in the Negative Conjugation of the Brahui Verb System. Journal of South Asian Linguistics 3(1).
sources.quote: No rule stated; stress marked per word with acute accent from 1990-91 fieldwork (e.g. bánning 'to come', báffing vs bafáng 'not to come', 'the stress is shifted to the stem' / 'the stress remains on the á'), showing morphologically conditioned stress placement in verb forms, consistent with Bray sec. 203 and with the record's 'exceptions pervasive'.
